subject: Token flow contract exception request — streaming vs sync commitments
messages:
From: Audrey Chen <audrey@payline.com>
To: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>
Date: 2028-04-01T09:12:00Z
Subject: Token flow & contract exception: streaming vs sync

Hi Monica,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We're getting close to internal approval but Legal pushed back on the streaming commitments in the draft SLA: specifically Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) guarantees and tokens-per-second sustained throughput for streaming endpoints.

For our billing and latency-sensitive UX we need clearer language on:
- How TTFT is measured (first-byte vs first-token vs first-chunk)
- Whether streaming endpoints are held to the same sustained tokens/sec targets as non-streaming (sync) endpoints, or if a carveout applies during high-concurrency bursts

They asked if Redwood would accept an exception that:
1) allows a 300ms variance window for TTFT on streaming in exchange for a lower per-token unit price; and
2) guarantees a lower sustained tokens/sec for streaming endpoints but commits to a fast fallback to a compatible sync endpoint when sustained rate thresholds are exceeded.

Can you confirm whether Redwood can sign with those two carveouts? If so, Legal will draft the exception language and circle back.

Thanks,
Audrey Chen
Head of Integrations
PayLine Inc.

Attachment: payline_streaming_profile.csv (sample traffic shapes)

From: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>
To: Audrey Chen <audrey@payline.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: 2028-04-01T11:05:00Z
Subject: Re: Token flow & contract exception: streaming vs sync

Hi Audrey —

Appreciate the clear asks and the traffic sample — that helps. Short answers up front: 1) yes, we can discuss a TTFT measurement window for streaming, and 2) we typically treat sustained tokens/sec differently for streaming vs sync and are open to a carveout that pairs a lower sustained guarantee with automatic fallback behavior.

I've looped in Karthik (contracts/infra) to scope the operational risks and Marissa on support/SLAs to outline fallout for observability and incident response.

Can Legal share the exact exception wording they prefer? To be efficient, Karthik and I propose two options:
A) TTFT defined as time to first-token emitted to client 95th percentile over monthly windows, with an allowable variance of up to 300ms for streaming endpoints; sustained tokens/sec for streaming set to X (lower) with automatic routing to a compatible sync model when 1-minute sustained threshold is exceeded.
B) Same TTFT measurement but no automatic fallback — instead a credit-backed remedy for sustained rate violations.

We prefer A operationally (fallback reduces prolonged user impact), but both are workable. I'll put together a short draft exception and share.

- Monica
Monica Patel
Head of Solutions — Redwood Inference

Attachment: redwood_sla_exception_request_v1.pdf

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>, Audrey Chen <audrey@payline.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2028-04-02T14:22:00Z
Subject: Re: Token flow & contract exception: streaming vs sync

Thanks Audrey & Monica — quick technical clarifications from infra side:

1) TTFT: We measure "first-token" as the first application-level token delivered by the streaming protocol to the client, not TCP first byte. For SLOs we calculate p95 over a rolling 30-day dataset by endpoint.

2) Variance window: 300ms is reasonable as a dev/testable target; however, the effective observed delta depends on model type, sequence length, and whether KV-cache prefix hits are present. For PayLine's traffic profile (see CSV) we estimate the p95 delta to sit between 150-350ms on g4dn-class hosts; on dedicated GPU pools with optimized kernels it'll be lower.

3) Sustained throughput: streaming endpoints are more sensitive to concurrency; we typically publish a lower sustained tokens/sec guarantee for streaming endpoints (we can call this "streaming sustained rate" R_stream) and a higher sustained rate for sync (R_sync). The automatic fallback option means: when a 60s sliding window detects sustained rate > R_stream, we can transparently route new requests to a sync-compatible variant or enqueue with backpressure. This will add complexity around KV-cache warm starts and may change per-request latency for the affected clients for the duration of the pressure event.

Operational ask: if Legal wants fallback semantics, we need explicit wording granting Redwood permission to route or downgrade to a compatible model, and SLAs on cache-warming time/expected latency delta. Otherwise we'll need a credit-remedy clause.

I'll also note cost tradeoffs if PayLine chooses to prioritize lower per-token pricing in exchange for a broader variance window — we can model that into the quote.

-Karthik
VP, Serving Infrastructure

From: Audrey Chen <audrey@payline.com>
To: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
Cc: PayLine Legal <legal@payline.com>
Date: 2028-04-02T16:03:00Z
Subject: Re: Token flow & contract exception: streaming vs sync

Thanks Karthik — very helpful. Legal prefers option A (fallback) because it reduces long tail user-visible failures, but they will include specific language requiring:
- A maximum cache warm-start latency of 2s for routed requests, counted separately from TTFT;
- A clause that credits are available if fallback results in >10% degradation in observed success rate for a given monthly window.

They asked for Redwood to propose precise numeric values for R_stream, R_sync, and the 1-minute sustained threshold based on our submitted traffic CSV. Can you run that estimation and return putative numbers so Legal can bake them into the exception?

Audrey

From: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>

Audrey — good. Karthik and Aditya will run the estimation against PayLine's CSV and propose numeric R_stream / R_sync / threshold by EOD tomorrow. Marissa and I will draft the exception wording for Option A including the cache-warm SLA (2s) and the credit trigger (>10% degradation).

Next steps summary:

- Redwood (Monica, Marissa): short exception draft for Legal including fallback definition, cache-warm SLA, monitoring/alerts, and credit mechanics.
- PayLine Legal: circulate draft internally; share redlines.

I'll upload the exception draft to the HubSpot deal and cc here when ready.

Thanks everyone — looking forward to closing this bit.

- Monica
Head of Solutions — Redwood Inference
